auditScope: Selections orders 11–20 as currently listed in docs/design/odysseys/church-of-rome.json. This is source collection, not scenario or architecture approval.

episodes.sourceAndBias: The selection's New Advent URL is an entry on the Henoticon, not the Acacian Schism. The consulted CCEL passage is Philip Schaff's 19th-century confessional church history, secondary and Protestant. New Advent's Hormisdas biography is Catholic Encyclopedia (1910). Neither was treated as a contemporary primary act in this audit.
episodes.coverageActuallyRead: Read Schaff section 'Beginning of Victory for Orthodoxy' lines 3–16: negotiations, 28 March 519 formula signature by Patriarch John, removal of Anastasius/Zeno from diptychs, and uneven local reception including Thessalonica. Search/opened the Catholic Encyclopedia Hormisdas summary reporting formula and communion settlement; not a critical edition of Hormisdas' letters or signed formula.
episodes.supportedClaim: Secondary accounts support reconciliation of communion in 519 under Justin I/Hormisdas, John II's acceptance of the formula and removal of names from diptychs. They also indicate the settlement's implementation was not uniform or frictionless.
episodes.dateAndPlaceLimits: Schaff gives 28 March in Constantinople; earlier design research notes alternate chronology/celebration dating (March 28 versus Easter/March 24 in some summaries). Treat exact ceremony date with source attribution pending a critical primary dossier. 'Rome and Constantinople reconcile' overstates universal ecclesiastical agreement: some eastern provinces and communities remained outside communion or contested implementation. The source supplies city-level Constantinople, not exact cathedral footprint/logistics.
episodes.qualification: Replace the incorrect candidate URL with the consulted reference and seek Hormisdas' letters/formula and John II's subscription before presenting exact documentary logistics as directly verified.

episodes.sourceAndBias: Liber Pontificalis, Life of John I, is a papal biography with confessional framing and hagiographic narrative; consulted through Duchesne's 19th-century edition/translation scan. Treccani's modern scholarly biography notes source disagreements. The candidate EGW passage is a later denominational narrative and was not used as evidence.
episodes.coverageActuallyRead: Liber Pontificalis scan pp. 157–160 (web PDF lines 4656–4838): Theodoric summons John to Ravenna and sends him to Justin at Constantinople; the mission, return, imprisonment/death story and politically loaded descriptions are present. Treccani lines 51–55: return after Easter 526, arrest/imprisonment at Ravenna, death date 18 May uncertain as to cause, and burial date disagreement.
episodes.supportedClaim: The LP reports Theodoric's embassy via Pope John I to Constantinople and John's later imprisonment/death at Ravenna. Treccani supports that the mission returned in 526 and cautions on death/burial chronology and cause.
episodes.dateAndPlaceLimits: The LP dates John’s tenure by consular years 523–526 but presents embassy chronology narratively; Treccani says the return was after Easter 526. Death in prison is reported, but whether travel hardships or detention caused it is uncertain. The selection's 525–526 is safer than a precise travel-day. Rome, Ravenna, Constantinople are broad locations; no specific prison or route footprint established.
episodes.qualification: The LP depicts both sides in confessional terms and claims sweeping outcomes; do not treat its diplomatic success narrative or Theodoric's alleged threat as impartial.

episodes.sourceAndBias: Procopius, Wars V (Gothic War I) XIV.14–17, near-contemporary campaign history by Belisarius' secretary; the narrative favors Roman military perspective. Consulted English Dewing translation (1914, Project Gutenberg) and checked the corrected LacusCurtius URL from the earlier source audit.
episodes.coverageActuallyRead: Gutenberg lines 543–551: Roman inhabitants invite Belisarius; he travels from Naples on the Latin Way; the Gothic garrison departs for Ravenna by permission of the Romans. Search result for the corrected LacusCurtius page identifies XIV.14–17 and Procopius' specific entry through Asinarian Gate with Goths leaving by Flaminian Gate on 9 December in Justinian's 11th regnal year.
episodes.supportedClaim: Procopius directly supports Belisarius entering Rome after an invitation and the Gothic garrison withdrawing to Ravenna; a different chapter's precise entry account names Asinarian and Flaminian gates.
episodes.dateAndPlaceLimits: 9 December 536 is a modern conversion of Procopius' regnal-calendar statement. Selection's Ostia label is anachronistically broad for the Rome entry; no occupation logistics in Ostia are demonstrated by the cited passage. The Latin Way/route is described at regional scale only. The original `War/5A*` URL is malformed for this edition; use the corrected Wars path or the accessible complete translation.
episodes.qualification: A source supports entry and garrison withdrawal, not a generic 'district supply' episode or exact modern street layout.

episodes.sourceAndBias: Procopius, Wars V–VI, near-contemporary Roman military narrative with strong campaign perspective; precise topographic details are useful but sometimes corrected by translator notes.
episodes.coverageActuallyRead: Read/located Wars V XIX–XXV and VI, including Procopius' chapter transition: the siege begins in March (V XXIV, as his discussion at lines 879–881 says it lasted until a year later); he ordered women, children, and nonessential attendants to leave for Campania, by boat from Rome's harbour or on the Appian Way (V XXV, lines 897–903); Book VI opening describes Gothic famine/pestilence and withdrawal (lines 1217 onward). Prior source audit checked chapter-level siege route and duration. Modern secondary search result gives Feb 537–Mar 538, not full article read.
episodes.supportedClaim: Protracted siege under Vitiges and Belisarius' defense are supported; civilians were evacuated from Rome toward Campania by sea/road under a rationing order; the Goths eventually abandoned the siege.
episodes.dateAndPlaceLimits: Procopius counts about a year and nine days; standard 537–538 interval is reconstructed, with month start sometimes stated Feb or Mar. His force/casualty totals and dialogue need attribution, not neutral acceptance. Boats in Rome's harbour are mentioned, but should not be automatically mapped to modern Ostia/Portus without a separate geography source. A translator footnote points out Procopius' gate-name error elsewhere; do not use every ancient place label as exact modern geometry.
episodes.qualification: The source attests civilian removal and siege hardship, but not an invented protected convoy or precise route corridor.

episodes.selectedDate: 546 CE (modern conversion; passage itself describes the event sequence)
episodes.sourceAndBias: Procopius, Wars VII (Gothic War III) XX.4–26, near-contemporary Roman campaign account. His sequence supplies details, but dramatic speeches, figures and motives remain a single historian's narrative.
episodes.coverageActuallyRead: Read §§4–26 (web lines 113–132): famine and weak guard; Isaurian guards negotiate with Totila; he enters through the Asinarian Gate at night; soldiers and some people flee; Procopius says only 500 common people remained, then reports killing, supplication by Pelagius, cessation of killing and unrestricted plunder. The earlier search extract for the selection's date came from a modern chronology summary, not a full thesis.
episodes.supportedClaim: Procopius supports Totila's capture of Rome through the Asinarian Gate and severe prior depopulation/famine; he specifically reports remaining soldiers/population, flight/refuge and plunder.
episodes.dateAndPlaceLimits: The date 546 (often 17 December) is reconstructed from chronology and not in the read passage. The '500' is Procopius' figure, not census data. The story supplies no archive extraction, named records store, or documented coordinated civilian refuge operation; `archive-extraction` is not historically established by this source. Gate and church names are ancient narrative locations, not exact current map footprints.
episodes.qualification: Avoid presenting dramatic dialogue, numbers, or motives as independent fact; distinguish documented capture/report from any invented archive mission.

episodes.sourceAndBias: Procopius, Wars VIII (Gothic War IV), near-contemporary campaign narrative. Britannica candidate was not opened in this pass. Prior embedded source audit reports Procopius VIII.33.26 for Narses' return/capture of Rome but did not expose exact passage in its inherited check; current opened VIII.33–35 covers Narses at Rome and final settlement/end of war.
episodes.coverageActuallyRead: Read LacusCurtius VIII.33–35 (web lines 29–84): Goths guarding Rome prepare resistance; after Totila's death, negotiations allow survivors to leave Italy with their own money and promise not to fight Rome; Procopius says the 18th war-year ended the Gothic War. Read the selected claim's underlying VIII.33.26 only as an inherited passage reference from the prior in-file audit, not independently line-verified here. Search result for VIII.33–35 gives further textual context.
episodes.supportedClaim: The read passage supports an eventual settlement and the end of the Gothic War after Narses' campaign; it indicates Narses was at Rome putting the city in order before the final settlement.
episodes.dateAndPlaceLimits: It does not prove that a single battle both 'restored imperial control over Rome and Italy' in 552–553: Narses' capture/entry of Rome, Taginae (552), and the final Gothic resistance/end (553) are separate stages. Rome is directly in narrative; no actual repair program is established by this passage. The listed geography `rome-ostia` should not imply Ostia-specific action. Month/day and broader consolidation need secondary chronology.
episodes.qualification: Keep capture, local restoration, and war's final end distinct; do not claim completed reconstruction from 'putting Rome in order'.

episodes.selectedDate: 593–595 CE; exact letter date not verified from passage
episodes.sourceAndBias: Gregory the Great, Registrum Epistolarum V.36, contemporary papal administrative correspondence. The 1895 English translation is in NPNF; the letter addresses Severus, a scholasticus connected to the Exarch.
episodes.coverageActuallyRead: Read the complete short letter (web lines 9–18): Gregory says Agilulf is willing to make general peace if the patricius/exarch agrees to arbitration of alleged violations by both sides; he warns that refusal may ruin islands and other places and asks for a truce to restore imperial forces.
episodes.supportedClaim: Direct support for Gregory advocating arbitration and a general peace between Agilulf and imperial authority, with mutual allegations and military/political stakes.
episodes.dateAndPlaceLimits: The page does not print a calendar date; Book V/chronological placement supports a mid-590s context, but selected 593–595 requires external epistolary chronology. It says 'his regions', islands and other places without naming a local negotiation site; Rome as the episode's map is not established. Letter describes advocacy, not proof peace agreement was concluded or implemented.
episodes.qualification: Keep this as a reported diplomatic proposal. Do not add a completed settlement, local battle or religious consensus.

episodes.selectedDate: 596–597 CE; dispatch and arrival are separate
episodes.sourceAndBias: Gregory the Great, Registrum VI.51 is near-contemporary correspondence to the missionaries; the translation is NPNF (1895). Bede, Ecclesiastical History I.25, is an eighth-century retrospective narrative written roughly a century later and carries providential/missionary framing.
episodes.coverageActuallyRead: Read Gregory VI.51 complete short letter and dating formula (web lines 9–18): he tells missionaries to continue, obey Augustine, who is returning to them; date is 10 Kalends August, 14th year of Maurice. Read Bede's Kent narrative lines 21–34: Thanet landing, audience with Æthelberht, provision for the mission, residence/preaching in Canterbury, and Roman-era church of St Martin. Fordham's selected Gregory URL was not accessible; consulted alternative primary translation and Bede separately.
episodes.supportedClaim: Gregory's letter directly supports mission organization/contact and Augustine's leadership, not first dispatch. Bede reports a 597 Kent arrival and royal permission for residence, sustenance and preaching; this is later narrative corroboration, not a contemporary eyewitness record.
episodes.dateAndPlaceLimits: The VI.51 date converts to July 596, consistent with a mission already underway; it does not date original departure from Rome. Bede dates arrival to 597 but his chronological scheme has known errors elsewhere; his precise Thanet geography and dialogue remain retrospective. Canterbury/Tanet are regional/place names, not proof of a modern landing point or exact Roman church footprint.
episodes.qualification: Do not collapse Rome's 596 dispatch/prologue and Kent's reported 597 arrival into one event or present Bede's speeches/miracles as verbatim neutral record.

episodes.sourceAndBias: Oxford University Cult of Saints entry reproduces Liber Pontificalis 69 in Latin and translation, with source-critical notes; LP short papal life is early seventh-century Roman narrative. Cambridge scholarly article (open text) interrogates the date/status and political reading of this entry.
episodes.coverageActuallyRead: Oxford lines 17–19 reproduce the entry: during Boniface's time he asked Phocas for the Pantheon and made it a church of Mary and all martyrs; lines 48–70 date evidence/activity bounds and identify Rome; lines 95–104 discuss composition, chronology, credibility limits. Cambridge article lines 580–582 says the conversion is now dated 13 May 613 rather than 609 and questions ownership/status; building may by then have been a secular public building, possibly used for judicial purposes.
episodes.supportedClaim: LP supports Boniface's request to Phocas and conversion/dedication of the Pantheon at Rome; Oxford identifies source as Latin text from the early 7th c. and gives the full short passage.
episodes.dateAndPlaceLimits: LP does not itself give the exact consecration day/year in this sentence. Scholarship differs: traditional 609 vs 13 May 613 argued by Cambridge article. LP's phrasing calls it templum, but it does not establish that active pagan rites were occurring or that pagan images were ceremonially removed at conversion. No precise staging/route or building work sequence is described.
episodes.qualification: Do not stage an icon-removal assault or assert an active cult purge from this source; retain the 609/613 dating disagreement. Oxford resource is CC0, but its reused translation still credits Davis/Duchesne.

episodes.sourceAndBias: Richard Price, Phil Booth and Catherine Cubitt, The Acts of the Lateran Synod of 649 (Liverpool University Press, 2014), scholarly edition/translation. JSTOR shows the book page and selected chapter extracts, but full book text is institutionally restricted. Price explicitly describes the published Acts as a redacted/propagandistic presentation rather than a straight factual record, while defending session authenticity.
episodes.coverageActuallyRead: Read JSTOR book metadata and description (lines 4–38), general introduction extracts (lines 94–135), and displayed extracts/section descriptors for Acts sessions (lines 161–227). The page supports five sessions from 5 to 31 October in the Lateran palace basilica and 106 bishops; it says both Greek and Latin versions are contemporary, Greek likely source text though business was in Latin, and the published Acts were intended to persuade. Full translation/session text was not available; TOC/abstract extracts only for most sessions.
episodes.supportedClaim: The edition page supports Pope Martin's synod in Rome at the Lateran from 5–31 October 649, five sessions, reported attendance of 106 bishops, and dispute over one/two wills and operations in Christ. The session headings show dates 5, 8, 17, 19, 31 October.
episodes.dateAndPlaceLimits: Selection says 106 bishops, while older sources often say 105; use this edition's figure with attribution. The synod rejected imperial doctrinal policy and is not proof of unanimous empire-wide reception; its Acts are openly advocacy/propaganda and Greek/Latin textual history is complicated. Lateran palace basilica is the documented venue, not proof of exact modern interior setup. Rome is the supported locality; Ostia does not enter this claim.
episodes.qualification: Mark the primary edition as only partially accessed: book description/introduction extracts, not full primary acts. Do not present doctrine or condemnations as neutral consensus.
